result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers make the same core fixes: focus moves to the first invalid field, errors are linked with aria-describedby and aria-invalid and announced through role='alert', the status div becomes a live region, old errors are cleared, the 1–12 party size is checked, and a failed request no longer shows 'Sent'. B also puts a short message in the status area next to the button, which is where people are looking when they think the button 'does nothing', so it tackles the actual complaint more directly with one small CSS rule. A has slightly clearer party-size wording and stops double submits, but both keep the bare 'Sent' and the vague 'Required'. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers make the same core fixes: focus moves to the first invalid field, errors are linked with aria-describedby and aria-invalid and use role='alert', old errors are cleared, the party-size range is checked, and 'Sent' only shows after an OK response. A adds an error summary next to the button, where users are actually looking. B disables the button while the request is sending and gives a more helpful failure message. Neither improves the bare 'Sent' or the generic 'Required' wording, so their strengths cancel out.
